question: “My name’s Elizabeth, but call me Liz.” Which name does she want you to use?
choices: Elizabeth’s family name.
Liz.
Your own first name.
Both names together.
note: “Call me Liz” gives you the name she likes to hear.

question: “This is Deniz. He lives next door.” Who is Deniz?
choices: Someone who lives beside you.
Someone who shares your room.
Someone who teaches your class.
Someone who goes to work with you.
note: “Next door” means in the home beside yours. A flatmate shares your flat.

question: At the photo club, Ada asks, “Is this your first time here?” What does she want to know?
choices: What time did you get here?
Did you arrive before everyone else?
Are you the first person on the list?
Have you been to this club before?
note: “My first time here” means I haven’t visited before. “What time?” asks about the clock.

question: “Mert and I are in the same class.” What do they share?
choices: One home address.
One seat on the bus.
One group of students.
One first name.
note: Students in the same class have lessons together. They can live in different places.

picture.alt: An open storybook with a little castle rising from its pages.

question: “I live near the university. How about you?” What does the speaker want to hear?
choices: How you feel today.
Where you live.
How big the university is.
Where you want to travel.
note: “How about you?” turns the same question back to you. Here the subject is home.

question: At a games club, three students are sitting around a table. There’s an empty chair. You’d like to play with them.
choices: Hi, I’m Can. Can I join you?
Hi, I’m Can. What game are you playing?
Are you waiting for another player?
Hi, I’m Can. Is this club open every week?
note: “Are you waiting for another player?” asks about the group. “Can I join you?” makes it clear you want to play.

picture.alt: A wooden game piece beside a die.

question: You’re having tea with Ada. Your cousin arrives. Ada looks at you because they’ve never met.
choices: Emre, would you like some tea?
Ada, have you two met before?
Ada, my cousin likes this café too.
Ada, this is my cousin Emre.
note: You know they haven’t met, so you can introduce Emre. “Have you two met before?” is useful when you’re unsure.

picture.alt: A cup of tea on a saucer with loose tea leaves nearby.

question: You’re writing a name on a welcome card. The new student tells you her family name, Kaya. You also need her first name.
choices: May I write Ms Kaya on the card?
Thanks. Is Kaya your family name?
Thanks. And what’s your first name?
Thanks. Would you like to write it yourself?
note: “Ms Kaya” is polite, but the card still needs her first name. If you only needed a surname, it would work.

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.

question: A student says, “We met at the photo club yesterday.” Now you remember him. What do you say?
choices: Hello! What’s your name again?
Oh yes! Good to see you again.
Hello! Do you take a lot of photos?
Hello! Lovely to meet you.
note: “Good to see you again” shows you remember him. “Lovely to meet you” usually starts a first meeting.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: You’re from İzmir and you now live in İstanbul. A new classmate asks, “Where are you from?”
choices: I’m from İzmir. I live here now.
I live near the station in İstanbul.
I’m going to İzmir this weekend.
I’m new here. Do you know the city well?
note: “From” asks about your home place. “I live near the station” answers a question about your home now.

picture.alt: A ferry beside an İstanbul skyline.

question: You play tennis every weekend. A new classmate says, “Tennis is my favourite sport.” You’d like to play together. What do you say?
choices: Mine too! Do you watch it on TV?
Mine too! Enjoy your game on Saturday.
Mine too! Where do you buy shoes?
Mine too! Shall we play on Saturday?
note: “Shall we play…?” invites her. “Enjoy your game” sounds as if she’s going to play without you.

picture.alt: A tennis racket and yellow ball.

question: At the start of your first class, the teacher smiles and says, “Hello, Deniz.” Your name is Demir. What do you say?
choices: Hello! Nice to meet you, too.
Hello! Shall I write my name on the board?
Hello! It’s Demir, with an m.
Hello! May I sit near the front?
note: “Nice to meet you” is friendly, but the teacher might keep calling you Deniz. Giving the correct name helps next time.

question: At the art club a visitor points to Eda and asks, “Is she the teacher?” Eda is a student. You know who the teacher is.
choices: Eda comes every Monday. Shall I introduce you?
She’s a student. That’s our teacher over there.
The teacher should be here. Shall we wait?
You can ask Eda. She knows the teacher.
note: You know who the teacher is and you can point her out. Sending the visitor to Eda would help if you were unsure.

question: A new student comes to choir practice alone. You know her name is Lea. She’s looking around for a place to sit.
choices: Hi, Lea. There’s a seat next to me.
Hi, Lea. Have you sung in a choir before?
Hi, Lea. I hope you enjoy singing here.
Hi, Lea. Would you like to look around first?
note: “I hope you enjoy singing here” welcomes Lea. Offering the seat also helps her settle in now.

question: After class you must leave to catch your bus. You’ve just met Sam and you’d like to talk again tomorrow.
choices: Would you like to get a coffee now, Sam?
It was nice talking to you. Bye!
What did you think of today’s class, Sam?
Nice talking to you. See you tomorrow!
note: “See you tomorrow” tells Sam you’d like to meet again. “Bye!” is a friendly way to finish without making plans.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.
